label: paragraph_title
text: HAUNTED HOUSES.

label: paragraph_title
text: ENCOUNTERS WITH GHOSTS.

label: text
text: Mr. Elliot O'Donnell, who has spent twenty-five years investigating the existence of ghosts, and frequently visits houses reputed to be haunted, interviewed recently by the "Morning Post," on Dr. Bernard Hollander's theory of ghosts, strongly disagreed with his suggestions.

label: text
text: "If," he said, "ghosts are merely energy created at the time of death, how does Dr. Hollander explain "prophetic" ghosts which warn people of approaching death, and sometimes appear when the person they represent is still alive? Further, ghosts will use violence and throw furniture about the room, something they could not do if they did not possess a personality of their own."

label: text
text: To the question, "Have you seen a ghost?" Mr. O'Donnell said definitely. "Yes." He seldom missed an opportunity of spending days and nights in haunted houses, and had seen and felt ghosts. They had tugged at him and pinched him, and a Banshee had been in his family for generations.

label: paragraph_title
text: GHOSTS YOUNG AND OLD

label: text
text:
He did not believe that they possessed one idea, which might keep them bound to one place. In any case, such a statement could not be proved. He knew of instances in which the ghost of a person had come back to some beloved place. He had known young ghosts and old ghosts, the ghosts of people of blameless character, and of others vulgarly termed wicked. They possessed a personality, either conscious or unconscious, outside that of human beings. Nor was it true in his opinion that people in an indifferent nervous state necessarily responded more easily to impressions. For his part he saw ghosts better when in good health.
"But," continued Mr. O'Donnell, "I do not believe in the ghosts created by mediums and seen at seances, I stand half-way between those who ascribe them to the operation of natural laws and those who put them in the world of spirits. That they appear to some people and not others I ascribe to the ghosts' own will in the matter. And that they appear dressed in clothes which we recognise is. I believe due to their desire to assist such recognition. It is their means of identity. On the other hand, I have seen a ghost half-human and half-animal, which I may mention was afterwards seen by a doctor who had no knowledge of my experience. That it should take this awful form I believe to be due to something

label: paragraph_title
text: STRANGE PROBLEM.

label: text
text: EXPRESS TRAIN MURDER

label: text
text: The prosecution rejects his story of an attack agd points out that the wounds to his head were no doubt sustained by his fall from the train, but the troubling fact remains that the third passenger in the fatal compartment had disappeared and has never revealed himself, while there is no trace of the identity papers which the victim certainly had. In his possession when he boarded the train at Marailles. Nearly a year of police investigation has failed to throw any further light on the affair, so that the answer to the riddle, if it be found at all, must be furnished by the jury.

label: text
text: The Vauclure Assize Court is called upon to solve a murder problem so difficult that it might have been invented by the most ingenious writer of detective stories. On May 12, 1914, Craisat, an engineer officer in the Greek mercantile marine, took a first-class ticket at Marseilles for Nice, but through misreading the platform signs he got into the wrong train and found himself speeding towards Paris in a compartment in which were two other passengers. He told the conductor of the train of his mistake and asked where he would be able to alight. The express had passed Avignon and was approaching the next station when a man was seen to jump out and run into a neighbouring field. It was Craisat, who was found badly wounded about the head. Meanwhile the conductor of the train, visiting the compartment in which Craisat had been travelling, found it occupied only by the dead body of one of his twofellow passengers, M. Bord, whose pocketbook and private papers had disappeared. Who killed him? Suspicion immediately fastened upon Craisat, and was strengthened when Bord's pocketbook was found in his possession. But Bord's identity papers were missing, and the third occupant of the compartment had also disappeared. Craisat declares that while he was sleeping he was awakened by violent blows on the head, and with his face covered with blood he rushed from the compartment and jumped out of the train to escape his assailant. He explains his possession of the pocketbook by saying that the man who attacked him and had murdered Bord must have placed it in his pocket so as to put the police on a false scent.
